summary: This bot builds one AsyncOpenAI client in OpenAIHelper.__init__ and uses it for everything. The vendored Router runtime now sits under that client, so all four chat.completions call sites - the chat turn, the image interpretation, the plugin follow-up and the history summarisation - are translated to Router's /v1/responses, while image generation, text-to-speech and Whisper transcription keep going to OpenAI on the same client because Router has no endpoint for them. Nothing changes until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set, and ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 turns it off again. Two things in the plugin path only worked because of OpenAI's Chat Completions wire format and had to be fixed: the bot stored a function result with no assistant turn asking for it (Router answers 400 'No tool call found for function call output', confirmed live, and the orphan stays in the chat's history so every later turn in that chat would fail too), and the streaming function-call detector gave up on Router's role-only opening chunk, so plugin calls were silently never run. With those fixed, the bot's own code was run end to end against the real Router: 20 of 20 requests served across plain chat, streaming chat, buffered and streamed plugin calls, a direct-result plugin, a second turn after a function call, image interpretation buffered and streamed, and summarisation. A side-by-side of all eleven paths against a stand-in OpenAI server shows the same answers, the same history and the same plugin flow on both routes.
reviewed: The review looked at every lever Router offers on /v1/responses against this bot's actual traffic - a Telegram chat that resends its whole history every turn, with a user waiting on each reply - and measured the ones that decide something on the real Router: prefix caching on gpt-4o, summarisation on gpt-4o vs gpt-4o-mini, a chat turn on gpt-4o vs gpt-5.1 at both tiers, image interpretation at the bot's 300-token cap on three models, and a fallback list falling through an unusable candidate. Six improvements came out of it, each on its own branch. Two ideas were measured and dropped: moving image interpretation to gpt-4o-mini (it bills 8,522 input tokens for an image gpt-4o bills at 277, so it costs more, not less) and billing user budgets from Router's usage.cost (the streaming paths never see a usage object, so it would make budget enforcement inconsistent) - both are recorded as notes.

items.title: Route the bot's chat traffic through Router
items.summary: The runtime goes under the one AsyncOpenAI client the bot builds, so its four chat.completions call sites are served by Router.
items.gains: All of the bot's text and vision traffic goes through one Router key, with per-call-site spend labels (metadata.feature) and every Responses lever available through router.policy.json. Chat Completions is translated to /v1/responses in both directions, including streaming and the legacy functions API, so no call site had to be rewritten.
items.price: no change on its own: the same model, at Router's list price, which matched usage.cost exactly in every live call measured here
items.why: One client serves everything in this codebase, so a single wrap at the construction site moves every chat call at once and leaves images, speech and transcription on OpenAI untouched - they share the client but Router has no endpoint for them. The runtime stays inert until RAMP_ROUTER_API_KEY is set, so this commit is safe to ship ahead of the switch, and ROUTER_MIGRATE_DISABLE=1 reverses it without a deploy. Deployments that point OPENAI_BASE_URL at another gateway keep working against that gateway: the runtime only routes api.openai.com.

evidence.detail: The bot's own code against the real Router: 20 of 20 requests served across plain chat, streaming chat, plugin function calls buffered and streamed, a direct-result plugin, a second turn after a function call, image interpretation buffered and streamed, and history summarisation.

All eleven paths run twice - against a stand-in OpenAI server with the runtime off, and against router-sim with it on. Same answers, same conversation history, same plugin flow; the only differences are the two stubs' own token-count formulas.
21 of 21 requests to router-sim valid, each tagged with its own feature label (__common_get_chat_response, __common_get_chat_response_vision, __handle_function_call, __summarise).
A custom OPENAI_BASE_URL deployment with the runtime active: 0 requests reached Router, all 11 paths still served by that host.
5 passed, the baseline count; bot/router_runtime.py and the edited bot/openai_helper.py also parse under Python 3.9, which is what the Dockerfile ships.

items.title: Keep plugin function calls working through Router
items.summary: Record the assistant turn that asks for a plugin call, and stop the streaming detector giving up on Router's role-only opening chunk.
items.gains: Plugin calls keep working on Router, buffered and streamed. Without this, a deployment with PLUGINS set would show its users a 400 on every function call and - because the orphaned function result stays in that chat's history - on every later turn of that chat as well, and streamed plugin calls would silently never run and return an empty reply.
items.loses: The assistant's function_call turn is now part of the conversation history, on OpenAI as well as on Router. That is a few tokens per plugin call and one more of the MAX_HISTORY_SIZE slots, so summarisation triggers marginally sooner in plugin-heavy chats. Measured on the stand-in server: a one-plugin turn went from 58 to 87 prompt tokens.
items.price: a few tokens per plugin call
items.why: The bot stored only the function result, never the assistant turn that asked for it. OpenAI tolerates that; Router does not, and it is the documented shape for the legacy functions API, so the fix is also what OpenAI asks for - the model now sees what it called, not just an unexplained result. The streaming half is the mirror image: the detector assumed OpenAI's habit of packing the assistant role and the first function_call fragment into one chunk, and Router sends the role on its own. It now skips chunks that carry nothing and replays whatever it read back to the caller, so a plain answer loses no text either way.

evidence.detail: Against the real Router: a function_call_output with no preceding function_call returns 400 'No tool call found for function call output with call_id call_legacy'; the same request with the assistant turn in front returns 200.

Before the fix, 2 of 8 paths differed (the buffered plugin call errored, the streamed one ran no plugin and answered empty). After it, all eleven paths match the stand-in OpenAI server, including a plugin whose result is sent straight to the user and a second user turn after a function call.
Live, the stub plugin's result reached the model and came back as an answer on both the buffered and the streamed path.
5 passed, the baseline count.

items.title: Image generation stays on OpenAI
items.summary: client.images.generate keeps going to OpenAI: Router serves no images endpoint.
items.loses: This traffic is not on the Router key, so DALL-E spend is not in Router's spend views and the OpenAI key must stay configured for it. The bot prices it itself from IMAGE_PRICES.
items.why: Router's endpoint list has no /v1/images/generations - it returns a plain-text 404. The call shares the wrapped client, and the runtime leaves it alone.

evidence.detail: router-migrate check --all: 'hard limit: images - Router has no endpoint for it'.

items.title: Speech and transcription stay on OpenAI
items.summary: TTS (audio.speech) and Whisper (audio.transcriptions) keep going to OpenAI: Router serves no audio endpoints.
items.loses: Voice-note transcription and spoken replies are not on the Router key, so that spend stays outside Router's views and the OpenAI key must stay configured. For a bot where every voice message is transcribed before it is answered, that is a real share of the traffic.
items.why: Audio is not in Router's endpoint list, and audio input on Responses returns 400 'Audio input is not available'. Both calls share the wrapped client and the runtime leaves them alone.

evidence.detail: router-migrate check --all: 'hard limit: audio - Router has no endpoint for it' on both sites.

items.title: Cache the repeated history prefix, label the spend
items.summary: A router.policy.json whose defaults set prompt_cache_key per call site and tag the spend with metadata.product.
items.gains: Every chat turn resends the whole conversation, so turn N+1's prompt begins with turn N's. A stable cache key per call site keeps that prefix landing where it is already cached. Measured on the real Router, gpt-4o, a 3,208-token prompt resent unchanged: 3,072 tokens served from cache and the turn's cost fell from $0.00816 to $0.00433 (-47%). metadata.product puts the bot's whole spend under one product in Router's views, next to the per-call-site feature labels the runtime already sends.
items.loses: Nothing in the answers: prompt_cache_key is an affinity hint, and the live samples returned the same content at the same latency. The one caveat is that my samples cannot separate the key's contribution from OpenAI's automatic prefix caching, which was already hitting without it - the -47% is the cache, and the key is there to make the hit reliable rather than to create it.
items.price: lower: up to -47% of a chat turn on the cached part of the prompt, growing with conversation length
items.why: This is the cheapest lever available to a bot whose prompt is mostly a prefix it already sent, and it changes no output. The labels cost nothing and make the next decision - which call site is actually expensive - answerable from Router's own views rather than from guesswork.

evidence.detail: gpt-4o, identical 3,208-token prompt sent twice: first call 0 cached, $0.00816; second 3,072 cached, $0.00433. With prompt_cache_key set, both calls hit cache at $0.00432.
The bot run against router-sim with this policy: all four features carry their own prompt_cache_key and metadata {feature, product}; 21 of 21 requests valid.
5 passed on the branch.

items.title: Bound how long a stuck upstream holds a chat
items.summary: provider_timeout of 60 s on the three calls a user waits on, 90 s on summarisation.
items.gains: The bot sets no timeout, so the OpenAI SDK's default applies - 600 s per attempt, with retries on top. A wedged upstream therefore holds the Telegram handler, and the user's chat, for minutes with neither a reply nor an error. provider_timeout gives Router a deadline per provider call; on a streamed call it is read as idle time between events, so a slow but live stream is not cut.
items.loses: A generation that would have finished late now ends as a plain-text 504 with no JSON body and no request id, which the bot surfaces as its generic error message. Long answers near the MAX_TOKENS ceiling are the ones at risk, and the timeout is a guess, not a measurement - it should be raised if real traffic starts hitting it.
items.price: no change, except that a timed-out attempt is still billed for what it generated
items.why: Every one of these calls has a human watching a chat window. A bounded failure the user can retry beats an unbounded wait, and 60 s is already far beyond this bot's measured response times (0.6-3.4 s in every live call here). Summarisation gets 90 s because it runs over a whole conversation and nothing is shown until it returns.

evidence.detail: The bot run against router-sim with this policy: provider_timeout 60 on the chat, vision and plugin features and 90 on summarisation, on the wire; 21 of 21 requests valid.
No upstream was slow enough to trigger a 504 during this work, so the cut-off path itself is unmeasured here; ROUTER.md records it as a plain-text 504.
5 passed on the branch.

items.title: Summarise long histories on gpt-4o-mini
items.summary: model_map on the summarisation call site only: gpt-4o becomes gpt-4o-mini.
items.gains: When a conversation outgrows MAX_HISTORY_SIZE the bot asks for a 700-character summary of it. Nobody reads that text; it only reseeds the history. Measured on the real Router with the bot's own prompt and a six-turn conversation: $0.00175 on gpt-4o against $0.000112 on gpt-4o-mini, a 94% cut, with both summaries carrying the same facts.
items.loses: A smaller model writes the summary that the rest of the conversation is built on, so detail can be lost on long or multilingual histories - and unlike a bad answer, that loss persists for the remainder of the chat. The map is keyed on gpt-4o, so a deployment running another OPENAI_MODEL is unaffected until its id is added.
items.why: It is the one call in this bot where output quality is almost invisible to the user and the model in use is the most expensive one available. Doing it in the policy rather than in the code means the bot's own token accounting, context-window maths and model-capability tables all keep working on gpt-4o - they never learn that Router served something else.

evidence.detail: The bot's summarisation prompt on a six-turn conversation: gpt-4o 200 in / 125 out, $0.00175; gpt-4o-mini 200 in / 136 out, $0.0001116. Both summaries name the same itinerary, the same train advice and the same food advice.
The bot run against router-sim with this policy: only the __summarise feature's requests carry model gpt-4o-mini; the other three stay on gpt-4o; 21 of 21 valid.
5 passed on the branch.

items.title: Serve the chat turns on gpt-5.1 instead of gpt-4o
items.summary: model_map on the chat turn and the plugin follow-up: gpt-4o becomes gpt-5.1.
items.gains: gpt-4o is this bot's default and the most expensive thing it runs. gpt-5.1 is cheaper on every axis that matters here: input $2.50 to $1.25 per 1M, cached input $1.25 to $0.125, and it has a Flex tier the account default already serves it at. Measured live on the same question: gpt-4o $0.0031925, gpt-5.1 at standard $0.0017750, gpt-5.1 at Flex $0.0009225 - a 71% cut - and gpt-5.1 answered in 173 output tokens where gpt-4o took 310. Cached input is where this bot spends most of its money, and that line is ten times cheaper.
items.loses: A different model answers every message: in these samples gpt-5.1 was consistently terser and heavier on markdown, so the bot's voice changes and anyone comparing it with the old deployment will notice. It is reasoning-capable, so some turns will bill reasoning tokens as output. And Flex is the account default for it: a streamed attempt falls back to standard after about 25 s, but a buffered one - voice replies, /chat - has no such guard, and one Flex call elsewhere has been seen to take 61 s. Pinning "service_tier": "default" in this entry opts out of Flex and keeps the standard-tier price.
items.price: -44% at the standard tier, -71% at the Flex tier the account default uses, on a like-for-like question
items.why: The bot's model is a 2024 default that has simply been overtaken: a newer model is half the input price, a tenth of the cached-input price, and answers more concisely. Doing it as a policy model_map rather than by changing OPENAI_MODEL matters here - default_max_tokens, are_functions_available, __max_model_tokens and __count_tokens are all hard-coded tables keyed on the configured id, and several of them raise NotImplementedError on an unknown model, so changing the env var would break the bot where changing the policy does not. Image interpretation and summarisation are deliberately left out: see i5 and i3.

evidence.detail: Same question, same settings: gpt-4o $0.0031925 (310 out, 2.6 s); gpt-5.1 service_tier default $0.0017750 (173 out, 3.1 s); gpt-5.1 at the account default tier, served Flex, $0.0009225 (180 out, 1.6 s). Every cost matched catalog list price exactly, and the Flex call was exactly half the standard one.

The whole bot, its own code, live against Router with this policy on: 20 of 20 requests served - plain chat, streaming chat, plugin function calls buffered and streamed, a direct-result plugin, and a second turn after one. Legacy functions translate and run on gpt-5.1.
Only the chat and plugin-follow-up features carry model gpt-5.1; vision and summarisation stay on gpt-4o; 21 of 21 valid.
5 passed on the branch.

items.title: Interpret images on gpt-5.1 instead of gpt-4o
items.summary: model_map on the image-interpretation call site: gpt-4o becomes gpt-5.1.
items.gains: Half the cost and a fuller answer. Measured live at the bot's own 300-token cap: a simple image $0.0008125 on gpt-4o against $0.000329 on gpt-5.1, a dense chart $0.0028975 against $0.001467. gpt-5.1 also tokenises the images smaller (231 and 651 input tokens against 277 and 787) and described the chart in more detail.
items.loses: Latency on a complex image: 5.2 s on gpt-5.1 against 2.0 s on gpt-4o, with a Telegram user watching for the reply. And gpt-5.1 is reasoning-capable while VISION_MAX_TOKENS is 300, so thinking tokens come out of the same budget as the answer; three samples all returned 0 reasoning tokens and a complete answer, but three samples do not prove it for every image. If image replies ever come back empty, raise VISION_MAX_TOKENS or undo this.
items.price: -59% on a simple image, -49% on a dense one
items.why: This is the same swap as i4, held back and measured separately because the vision call is the one place where the bot's output cap is small enough for a reasoning model to spend it on thinking and return nothing. The measurement says that did not happen, so the saving is available - but it is a different risk from the chat swap and deserves its own yes or no.

evidence.detail: At max_output_tokens 300, on a simple image and a dense chart: gpt-4o $0.0008125 (12 out, 1.3 s) and $0.0028975 (93 out, 2.0 s); gpt-5.1 $0.000329 (37 out, 0.8 s) and $0.001467 (212 out, 5.2 s). All four completed, none incomplete, 0 reasoning tokens throughout.
Only the vision feature's requests carry model gpt-5.1; the other three stay on gpt-4o; 21 of 21 valid.
5 passed on the branch.

items.title: Give the user-facing calls a fallback model
items.summary: A models list on the chat, vision and plugin-follow-up call sites: gpt-4.1, then claude-haiku-4-5.
items.gains: Today an upstream failure reaches the user as the bot's generic error. A models list lets Router try the next candidate instead - gpt-4.1 first, same vendor and same request shape, then claude-haiku-4-5, so an OpenAI-wide problem is not the end of the conversation. The plugin follow-up keeps only gpt-4.1, to stay on the vendor whose legacy function-call translation this path was measured against.
items.loses: When a fallback fires, a different model answers and nothing in the reply says so: the bot's voice changes mid-conversation and the price becomes that candidate's. Router does not fall back once a stream has started and STREAM defaults to true, so this covers failures up to the first token, not mid-answer. Truncated attempts are still billed, and Router's policy guard silently drops any candidate that cannot take the request's tools, image or temperature, so a list can be shorter than it looks.
items.price: no change until a fallback fires, then the serving candidate's price (gpt-4.1 $2/$8, claude-haiku-4-5 $1/$5 per 1M against gpt-4o's $2.50/$10)
items.why: A chat bot has no queue and no retry of its own: a failed call is a failed conversation. This is the one lever that turns an upstream outage into a slightly different answer instead of an error, and it costs nothing while everything is healthy. It is listed last because its reach is genuinely limited by streaming.

evidence.detail: A models list whose first candidate this key cannot use ([gemini-2.5-flash, gpt-4o-mini]) fell through and was answered by gpt-4o-mini; a healthy list ([gpt-4o, gpt-4.1-mini]) was answered by gpt-4o.
The whole bot, its own code, live against Router with the lists in place: 20 of 20 requests served, each chat, vision and plugin request carrying models instead of model.
On the wire: chat and vision carry [gpt-4o, gpt-4.1, claude-haiku-4-5], the plugin follow-up [gpt-4o, gpt-4.1], summarisation is untouched; 21 of 21 valid.
5 passed on the branch.

items.title: gpt-4o-mini is the wrong cheap model for images
items.summary: Measured: gpt-4o-mini bills 8,522 input tokens for an image gpt-4o bills at 277, so it costs more, not less.
items.price: gpt-4o-mini $0.0012891 against gpt-4o $0.0009025 for the same image and prompt
items.why: The obvious way to make image interpretation cheaper is to send it to the mini model, and the catalog price ($0.15/$0.60 against $2.50/$10) makes that look like a 94% saving. It is not: gpt-4o-mini uses a far higher image token multiplier, so the same picture arrives as 8,522 input tokens instead of 277 and the call ends up more expensive than gpt-4o. It would also put the bot's own __count_tokens_vision estimate (85 + tiles x 170) badly out, which feeds user budgets. i5 proposes gpt-5.1 instead, which is genuinely cheaper on measured tokens.

evidence.detail: Same JPEG, same prompt, max_output_tokens 300: gpt-4o 277 input tokens $0.0009025; gpt-4o-mini 8,522 input tokens $0.0012891; gpt-5.1 231 input tokens $0.000304.

items.title: User budgets are priced from TOKEN_PRICE, not Router's cost
items.summary: The bot charges budgets at a flat TOKEN_PRICE per 1k tokens; Router reports the real cost per request and the bot ignores it.
items.price: TOKEN_PRICE defaults to $0.002 per 1k tokens; gpt-4o actually costs $0.0025 in and $0.010 out per 1k
items.why: USER_BUDGETS and GUEST_BUDGET are enforced from a price the operator types into the environment, which already understates gpt-4o and would drift further after any model swap (i3, i4, i5). Router returns the true figure: usage.cost is on every Responses reply and the runtime passes it through on the translated Chat Completions object, so response.usage.cost is readable today at the two buffered call sites. I did not build this: the streaming paths never get a usage object at all (the bot counts those tokens locally with tiktoken), so billing some turns from Router's cost and others from an estimate would make budget enforcement less consistent, not more. Worth doing properly together with a decision about what the streaming paths should do - and in the meantime, Router's own spend views, now labelled per call site and per product, are the accurate source.

evidence.detail: usage.cost was present and exactly matched catalog list price on all 12 buffered live calls measured here, across gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini and gpt-5.1.

items.title: Configurations that keep traffic on OpenAI
items.summary: Four supported settings make the runtime leave requests with the provider; all of them keep working, none of them reach Router.
items.price: no change: those requests are billed by OpenAI as before
items.why: Worth knowing before reading Router's spend views and concluding traffic is missing. N_CHOICES above 1 (the runtime cannot express n on Responses), a non-zero PRESENCE_PENALTY, an OPENAI_MODEL that is not a Router catalog id - of the models this bot's own tables list, gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4, gpt-4-turbo, gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini and o1 are in the catalog while gpt-3.5-turbo-16k, gpt-4-32k, chatgpt-4o-latest, o1-mini and o1-preview are not - and OPENAI_BASE_URL pointing at another gateway, which the runtime deliberately does not touch. In each case the request goes to the provider exactly as it did before.

evidence.detail: With the runtime active and OPENAI_BASE_URL pointing at a stand-in host, 0 of the bot's requests reached Router and all 11 paths were served by that host.
Catalog membership checked against the live GET /v1/models snapshot taken for this migration.
